This behavior suggests that $ a(n) $ is closely related to the **number of bits** required to represent $ n $ in binary. Specifically, $ a(n) $ is equal to the **floor of the base-2 logarithm of $ n $** plus 1, i.e.,

$$
a(n) = \left\lfloor \log_2(n) \right\rfloor + 1 \quad \text{for } n \geq 1.
$$

However, we are asked to express this as a **recurrence relation**. A natural way to define this sequence recursively is to observe that dividing $ n $ by 2 (integer division) reduces the number of bits by 1. Therefore, we can define the recurrence as follows:

---

### **Recurrence Relation**

$$
a(n) = 
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } n = 0, \\
a\left(\left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{2} \right\rfloor\right) + 1 & \text{if } n \geq 1.
\end{cases}
$$

---

### **Alternative Form (Splitting into Even and Odd Cases)**

To avoid the use of the floor function, we can express the recurrence in terms of whether $ n $ is even or odd:

$$
a(n) = 
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } n = 0, \\
a\left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right) + 1 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}, \\
a\left(\dfrac{n - 1}{2}\right) + 1 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}.
\end{cases}
$$
